props.title: The Last Days of Frankie the Fly
props.initialSlug: Small-time bookie aims for Hollywood glory

sections.content: The Last Days of Frankie the Fly (1996) represents an overlooked neo-noir gem featuring Dennis Hopper at his unhinged best. The film follows the seedy underbelly of Los Angeles through the eyes of a small-time bookie who dreams bigger than his station allows. It shares thematic DNA with other 90s crime dramas like Bad Lieutenant (1992) and The Last Seduction (1994), exploring the destructive nature of ambition in the criminal underworld. Director Peter Markle channels the gritty aesthetic of classic noir while incorporating the explicit violence that defined 90s crime films.

sections.content: The film sits within a specific subset of 1990s crime movies that merged classic noir elements with exploitation cinema aesthetics. Like Romeo Is Bleeding (1993) and Things to Do in Denver When You're Dead (1995), it features character actors given rare leading roles in stories about small-time criminals way over their heads. Hopper's performance as Frankie echoes his work in Blue Velvet (1986), bringing that same unstable energy to a more sympathetic character.

The film's treatment of the adult film industry parallels other 90s works like Boogie Nights (1997), though with a darker, more cynical lens. The relationship between crime and pornography became a recurring theme in 90s neo-noir, reflecting anxieties about the commercialization of sex and violence in American culture. movies.slug: A group of criminals face deadly consequences after a job goes wrong

sections.content: While major neo-noir films like L.A. Confidential (1997) and Miller's Crossing (1990) received critical acclaim and larger audiences, smaller productions like The Last Days of Frankie the Fly often pushed the genre's boundaries further. These films frequently incorporated elements of exploitation cinema and pulp fiction, creating hybrid works that reflected the decade's fascination with sex, violence, and moral ambiguity.
